rows.verified: Incorrect altimeter pressure settings during instrument approaches can create controlled-flight-into-terrain risk.
CAA Safety Notice SN-2023/003 is current and highlights CFIT risk during BARO-VNAV and two-dimensional approaches.
CAA guidance describes monitoring techniques to avoid inadvertent CFIT while receiving an air-traffic service or radar vectors.
Controlled flight into terrain is a major aviation hazard, particularly during approach operations.
Continuous-descent final-approach techniques can reduce destabilising level segments and changes close to the ground.
Pilot performance and situational awareness are central mitigations for CFIT outcomes.
Mountain flying requires deliberate terrain-clearance margins, route planning and consideration of downdrafts and mountain waves.
Operators and pilots should use current procedures, altimeter-setting discipline, monitoring and go-around criteria to preserve terrain clearance.
CFIT risk depends on terrain, procedure, altimeter setting, navigation, weather, aircraft performance, crew monitoring and air-traffic service.
CAA CFIT evidence is aircraft-, procedure-, crew-, terrain-, weather- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level accident probability.
The integrity of railway structures, earthworks, operational property and drainage is fundamental to safe railway operation.
Failure of civil-engineering assets can obstruct or distort track and lead to derailment.
Structural collapse or falling components can injure staff, passengers and members of the public.
Earthwork, drainage and structure failures may occur suddenly during extreme or highly localised weather.
Dutyholders should maintain accurate asset, condition and risk information.
ORR expects risk-based renewal, refurbishment, maintenance and consequence-management decisions.
Remote monitoring and engineering innovation can strengthen management of vulnerable assets.
Railway civil-engineering risk must be managed as a system because drainage, earthworks, structures and track are interdependent.
Rail-civils risk depends on asset age, condition, hidden defects, drainage, weather, loading, inspection, monitoring and mitigation.
ORR civil-engineering evidence is asset-, route-, weather-, inspection-, mitigation- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level derailment probability.
